answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer): In the Psychology replication project (RPP) in this dataset, roughly 46% of successfully replicated studies were led (most senior author of the replication team) by a junior professor — 16 of the 35 studies with replicated = 1 have a most-senior replication author of Assistant Professor (10) or Assistant (6). Junior-led replication teams are thus well represented among successful replications, though slightly under their share of all rpp replications (38/97 ≈ 39%... note the reverse: junior share among replicated, 45.7%, is somewhat higher than among all rpp studies, 39.2%), suggesting junior-senior-led teams did not differ dramatically in replication success.

Full sentence for submission: "Approximately 46% (16/35) of successfully replicated studies in the Psychology replication project (rpp) were led by a junior professor (most senior replication author an Assistant Professor or Assistant), with sensitivity variants ranging from about 52% to 58% depending on whether 'Researcher' is counted as junior and whether the 7 undocumented drop-flagged rows are excluded."

WORKFLOW: Loaded meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows, 141 unique O/R pairs; second file excluded as it contains no seniority/author columns). Restricted to project == "rpp" (97 rows = 97 unique ids, one row per O/R pair; lab_id/aggregated all NaN, so no lab-level duplication). Used the existing replicated == 1 binary column as the replication outcome (spot-check: identical to the derived p_value.r <= 0.05 & same-direction rule on all 94 rows with the needed fields; 3 rows lack p_value.r/ES inputs). Used seniority.r (most senior author of the replication team; the metadata's "original paper" wording treated as a typo). Junior = {Assistant Professor, Assistant}; Professor/Associate Professor = senior; Researcher excluded from junior in the primary. Numerator/denominator computed on all 97 rpp rows (drop==True rows kept in the primary per approved spec). Sensitivity variants recomputed as below; no seniority values were missing anywhere in rpp.

PRIMARY RESULT: 16/35 = 45.7% of replicated rpp studies led by a junior professor.
Replicated (n=35) seniority breakdown: Assistant Professor 10, Professor 8, Associate Professor 7, Assistant 6, Researcher 4.

SENSITIVITY TABLE (proportion junior among replicated rpp studies):
| Variant | Junior def. | Rows | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| PRIMARY (approved) | Assistant Professor + Assistant | all 97 | 16/35 = 45.7% |
| Junior incl. Researcher | + Researcher | all 97 | 20/35 = 57.1% |
| drop==True excluded | Assistant Professor + Assistant | 90 | 16/31 = 51.6% |
| Incl. Researcher, drop excluded | + Researcher | 90 | 18/31 = 58.1% |
| Secondary: seniority.o | Assistant Professor + Assistant | all 97 | 0/35 = 0.0% |
Context (all 97 rpp rows, not the headline denominator): junior = 38/97 = 39.2%; seniority.r counts: Associate Professor 24, Assistant Professor 23, Professor 19, Researcher 16, Assistant 15.

DIAGNOSTICS / FLAGS per the refinement request: (1) The 7 drop==True rpp rows (rpp.154, rpp.46, rpp.59, rpp.69, rpp.73, rpp.77, rpp.82) are NOT duplicates or degenerate rows — each has a unique id, complete seniority and replicated values; the rationale for the drop flag is undocumented in the data, hence they are retained in the primary per your instruction. (2) The 786 duplicated ids in the full file are entirely the ml1/ml3 lab-level structure (up to 37 rows per id); rpp has none. (3) The seniority.o secondary variant (0/35) reflects that in rpp the original papers' senior authors were almost all Professors (83/97), confirming seniority.o is not the intended variable for "junior professors in replicated studies."

LIMITATIONS: (i) "junior" has no ground-truth definition; the primary choice {Assistant Professor, Assistant} is a judgment call, with Researcher-treated-as-junior raising the estimate to ~57%. (ii) The drop flag's meaning is unknown; excluding those rows shifts the estimate to ~52%. (iii) seniority.r captures only the single most senior replication author, not the full author team. The plausible range for the headline answer is ~46–58%, centered on 45.7% under the approved primary specification.

payload.primary: 16/35 = 45.7% of replicated rpp studies led by a junior professor (Assistant Professor or Assistant, by seniority.r)
